lessons.title: Variables
lessons.summary: Giving values names with local, changing them, and why almost every variable should be local.

sections.heading: A name for a value
sections.body:
A **variable** is a name that points at a value. Once you've named something, you can use the name instead of repeating the value, and if the value changes, every use of the name sees the new value.

You create one with the word `local`, a name, an equals sign, and a value. The equals sign doesn't mean "is equal to" like in maths. It means "store this value under this name", which is why it's called **assignment**.

example.caption: Creating and using variables
example.code:
local customer = "Mrs Hill"
local pizzas = 2
print(customer, "ordered", pizzas, "pizzas")
example.explain: Prints `Mrs Hill ordered 2 pizzas`. The names stand in for their values.

sections.heading: Changing a variable
sections.body:
After a variable exists, assign to it again **without** `local` to change its value. Writing `local` a second time creates a brand new variable with the same name, which hides the old one. That's legal, but it's almost never what you meant, and it causes confusing bugs.

Assignment works right to left: Luau works out the value on the right first, then stores it. That's why a line can use a variable's old value to calculate its new one, like adding one to a counter.

example.caption: Updating a counter
example.code:
local deliveries = 0
deliveries = deliveries + 1
deliveries = deliveries + 1
print(deliveries)
example.explain: Prints `2`. Each line reads the old value, adds one, and stores the result.

sections.heading: Naming rules and style
sections.body:
Names can use letters, digits and underscores, but can't start with a digit, and can't be one of Luau's keywords like `end`, `local` or `if`. Names are case-sensitive, so `score` and `Score` are different variables.

Good names say what the value means: `deliveryCount` beats `d`, and `isNight` beats `flag`. Most Roblox scripters write their own variables in camelCase, starting lowercase and capitalising each later word. A name you can read aloud and understand is worth the extra letters.

sections.heading: Why local
sections.body:
If you assign to a name that was never declared with `local`, Luau creates a **global** variable instead. Globals work, but they're slower to look up, they can be changed from anywhere in the script, and a typo silently creates a new global rather than causing an error you'd notice.

So the rule is simple: declare every variable with `local`. Studio's Script Analysis window flags unknown globals, which catches many typos before you press Play.

A variable you declare but never assign starts as `nil`, Luau's value for "nothing". You can also declare several at once, with matching values on the right: two names, a comma, then two values.

key_points: `local name = value` creates a variable. Assign again without `local` to change it.
Assignment stores the right-hand value under the left-hand name.
Names are case-sensitive and should describe the value.
Always use `local`. Globals are slow and hide typos.
mistakes: Writing `local` again when updating a variable, which creates a second variable instead.
Misspelling a variable, so Luau reads a different name that's `nil`.
Leaving out `local` and accidentally creating a global.
lessons.try_it: Create variables for a customer's name, their house number and how many pizzas they ordered, then print a sentence using all three. Change one value with a second assignment and print again.

quiz.question: What does this print? `local tips = 5` then `tips = tips + 3` then `print(tips)`
quiz.explain: The second line reads 5, adds 3 and stores 8 back in tips.

quiz.question: Which is a valid variable name?
quiz.explain: Names can't start with a digit, can't contain dashes (that's subtraction), and can't be keywords like end.

quiz.question: Why should you use `local` for your variables?
choices: Locals are faster and a typo can't silently create a new global
Locals can hold more kinds of values
Without local, the value is always nil
quiz.explain: Globals do work, but they're slower and make typos harder to spot.

lessons.title: Numbers and maths
lessons.summary: Luau's arithmetic operators, the order they run in, and the quirks of decimal numbers.

sections.heading: The arithmetic operators
sections.body:
Luau has one number type that holds both whole numbers and decimals. You do maths with these operators: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies, `/` divides, `^` raises to a power, `%` gives the remainder, and `//` divides and rounds down.

Plain division always gives the exact answer, so `7 / 2` is `3.5`. When you only want whole results, like how many full boxes you can fill, use floor division: `7 // 2` is `3`.

sections.heading: Remainders are surprisingly useful
sections.body:
`%` (modulo) gives what's left over after dividing. `17 % 5` is `2`, because 5 goes into 17 three times with 2 left over. That makes it perfect for "every so often" logic: a number `n` is even when `n % 2` is `0`, and every fourth delivery is the one where `deliveries % 4` is `0`.

It also wraps values around. If a light cycles through 3 colours, adding one and taking the result `% 3` keeps it in the range 0 to 2 forever.

example.caption: Splitting slices fairly
example.code:
local slices = 26
local people = 4
print("Each gets", slices // people)
print("Left over", slices % people)
example.explain: Prints `Each gets 6` and `Left over 2`. Floor division and remainder work as a pair.

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.body:
Luau follows the usual maths order: powers first, then multiplication and division (including `//` and `%`), then addition and subtraction. Operators of the same level run left to right. So `2 + 3 * 4` is `14`, not `20`.

When in doubt, add brackets. `(2 + 3) * 4` is `20`, and brackets also make your intent obvious to the next person who reads the code. Brackets cost nothing, so use them whenever the order isn't instantly clear.

sections.heading: Decimals aren't exact
sections.body:
Computers store decimals in binary, and some simple-looking decimals can't be stored exactly. The classic example is `0.1 + 0.2`, which prints `0.30000000000000004` in Luau. That's not a Luau bug, it happens in almost every language.

The practical rules: don't compare decimals with exact equality, and round before you show them to players. Whole numbers are exact up to very large values, which is why things like money are often counted in whole units, such as cents, rather than as fractions of dollars.

You'll meet the `math` library, with rounding and much more, in chapter 7.

key_points: `+ - * / ^ % //` are Luau's arithmetic operators.
`/` gives exact results, `//` rounds down, `%` gives the remainder.
Powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Brackets override.
Decimals can be slightly off, so avoid exact comparisons with them.
mistakes: Expecting `7 / 2` to be `3`. Use `//` for whole-number division.
Forgetting precedence, so a total is calculated in the wrong order.
Checking whether a decimal sum equals an exact value.
lessons.try_it: Work out how many full boxes of 6 you can fill with 50 donuts and how many are left over, using `//` and `%`. Then print `2 + 3 * 4` and `(2 + 3) * 4` and explain the difference to yourself.

quiz.question: What is `15 // 4`?
quiz.explain: Floor division divides, then rounds down: 3.75 becomes 3.

quiz.question: What does `print(10 - 2 * 3)` show?
quiz.explain: Multiplication runs first: 2 times 3 is 6, and 10 minus 6 is 4.

quiz.question: Which expression is `0` exactly when `n` is a multiple of 5?
quiz.explain: The remainder after dividing by 5 is zero only for multiples of 5.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Writing text, joining it with .., measuring it, and converting between text and numbers.

sections.heading: Writing strings
sections.body:
A **string** is a piece of text. You write one between double quotes or single quotes; they mean the same thing, so pick whichever means you don't need to escape anything. For text that contains a double quote, wrap it in single quotes, or put a backslash before the inner quote.

The backslash starts an **escape sequence**: `\n` is a new line, `\t` is a tab, `\\` is a real backslash, and `\"` is a double quote that doesn't end the string. Text spread over several lines can go between double square brackets, which keeps the line breaks exactly as typed.

sections.heading: Joining strings with ..
sections.body:
Two dots join (or **concatenate**) values into one string. Unlike passing several values to `print`, concatenation adds **no** space, so include the spaces yourself.

Numbers can be joined too, and are turned into text automatically. Leave a space between a number and the dots, because Luau would otherwise read the first dot as a decimal point. You can't join `nil` or a boolean directly, though: that's an error. Convert those with `tostring` first.

example.caption: Building a message
example.code:
local house = 14
local street = "Elm Road"
local address = house .. " " .. street
print("Deliver to " .. address)
example.explain: Prints `Deliver to 14 Elm Road`. The middle string adds the space between the number and the street.

sections.heading: Length with #
sections.body:
Put `#` before a string to get its length, the number of characters (strictly, bytes, which is the same thing for plain English text). `#"pizza"` is `5`. It's handy for checks like "names must be at least 3 characters".

The `#` operator also measures lists, which you'll use constantly once you meet tables in chapter 6.

sections.heading: Converting between text and numbers
sections.body:
`tostring(value)` turns anything into text: `tostring(42)` is `"42"` and `tostring(true)` is `"true"`. `tonumber(text)` goes the other way, and gives back `nil` when the text isn't a number, so `tonumber("12")` is `12` but `tonumber("twelve")` is `nil`. That `nil` is useful: it's how you detect bad input.

Luau will also quietly turn a numeric string into a number during arithmetic, so `"5" + 3` is `8`. Don't rely on it. Convert explicitly, so your code says what it means and a non-number fails clearly instead of halfway through a sum.

You'll convert constantly in Roblox. Text from a player's TextBox is always a string, even when they typed digits, and attributes or saved data can arrive as either type. Converting at the point where a value enters your code, and checking for `nil` right there, keeps the rest of your script simple.

key_points: Strings go in single or double quotes. Backslash escapes like `\n` add special characters.
`..` joins values with no space added.
`#` gives a string's length.
`tostring` and `tonumber` convert, and `tonumber` returns `nil` for non-numbers.
mistakes: Forgetting spaces when concatenating, producing `Deliver to14`.
Concatenating `nil` or a boolean without `tostring`, which errors.
Writing `1..2` without spaces, which Luau reads as a malformed number.
lessons.try_it: Make variables for a customer's first and last name, join them into a full name with a space, and print the full name and its length. Then try `tonumber` on a few strings, including one that isn't a number.

quiz.question: What does `print("Slice" .. 3)` show?
quiz.explain: Concatenation turns the number into text and adds no space.

quiz.question: What is `tonumber("ten")`?
quiz.explain: tonumber returns nil when the text isn't a number, which lets you detect bad input.

quiz.question: What does `#"night"` give?
quiz.explain: The # operator gives a string's length: n, i, g, h, t.

lessons.title: Booleans, comparisons and nil
lessons.summary: true and false, the comparison operators that produce them, and what nil really means.

sections.heading: true and false
sections.body: A **boolean** is a value that's either `true` or `false`. Booleans are how code asks yes-or-no questions: is it night, has the order been paid, is the player hiding. You'll store them in variables with names that read like questions, such as `isNight` or `hasKey`, and in the next chapter you'll use them to make decisions.

sections.heading: Comparison operators
sections.body:
Comparisons produce booleans. `==` asks "are these equal", `~=` asks "are these different", and `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes. Note that equality uses **two** equals signs, because a single one means assignment, and that "not equal" in Luau is `~=`, not the `!=` used by some other languages.

Comparisons work on strings too. `==` checks the text matches exactly, including capitals and spaces, and `<` compares alphabetically, character by character.

example.caption: Comparisons give booleans
example.explain: Prints `true`, `false`, then `true`, since capital letters make the names different.

sections.heading: Comparing different types
sections.body:
Values of different types are never equal: `1 == "1"` is `false`, because a number isn't a string, even when they look alike. That catches people out when a value came from text, so convert first with `tonumber`.

Size comparisons between different types are worse: `1 < "2"` is an **error**, since Luau won't guess what you meant. If you see "attempt to compare number < string", one side is a string you expected to be a number.

sections.heading: nil means nothing
sections.body:
`nil` is the value that means "no value". A variable you never assigned is `nil`, and so is anything Luau looks up and doesn't find. It's not zero, and it's not an empty string: it's the absence of a value.

Most errors you'll ever see involve a `nil` turning up where you expected something real. You can test for it with `== nil` or `~= nil`.

`typeof(value)` tells you what type a value is, as a string: `"number"`, `"string"`, `"boolean"`, `"nil"`, and later `"table"`, `"function"` and Roblox types like `"Instance"`. When a value isn't behaving, printing its type is often the fastest way to find out why.

There are only two values Luau treats as "no" in a yes-or-no question: `false` and `nil`. Everything else counts as "yes", including `0` and the empty string. That surprises people coming from other languages, and it matters a lot in the next chapter, where conditions decide which code runs.

key_points: Booleans are `true` or `false`, and comparisons produce them.
`==` is equality, `~=` is not-equal. A single `=` is assignment.
Different types are never equal, and comparing their sizes is an error.
`nil` means no value. `typeof` tells you a value's type.
mistakes: Comparing a number with a string that only looks like a number.
lessons.try_it: Store a number of minutes in a variable and print whether it's more than 30, exactly 30, and not 45. Then print the type of a number, a string, a boolean and a variable you never assigned.

quiz.question: What does `print(5 == "5")` show?
quiz.explain: A number and a string are different types, so they're never equal.

quiz.question: Which operator means "not equal" in Luau?
quiz.explain: Luau uses a tilde followed by an equals sign.

quiz.question: What does `typeof(nothingHere)` give, if `nothingHere` was never assigned?
quiz.explain: Unassigned names are nil, and typeof returns the type name as a string.

lessons.title: Updating values
lessons.summary: Compound assignment like += and ..=, swapping values, and naming values that never change.

sections.heading: Compound assignment
sections.body:
Changing a variable based on its own value is so common that Luau has a shortcut. Instead of writing the name twice, as in adding one to `score` and storing it in `score`, you can write `score += 1`. It means exactly the same thing.

There's a version for every arithmetic operator: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `//=`, `%=` and `^=`, plus `..=` for adding text onto the end of a string. Luau doesn't have `++` like some languages, so `+= 1` is the way to count up.

example.caption: A running bill
example.code:
local bill = 0
bill += 12
bill += 12
bill *= 2
print(bill)
example.explain: Prints `48`: two 12s make 24, then doubling makes 48.

sections.heading: Building text step by step
sections.body:
`..=` adds onto the end of a string, which is useful for building messages a piece at a time, such as adding each item of an order to a receipt line.

It only works on a variable that already holds a string. If the variable is still `nil`, there's nothing to add onto, and you'll get an error, so start it as an empty string, two quotes with nothing between them.

For a handful of pieces this is fine. If you're joining hundreds of pieces in a loop, there's a faster tool, `table.concat`, which you'll meet with tables in chapter 6.

example.caption: Growing a message
example.code:
local note = "Order:"
note ..= " pepperoni"
note ..= ", garlic bread"
print(note)

sections.heading: Swapping and multiple assignment
sections.body:
You can assign several variables in one line by listing names on the left and values on the right, separated by commas. Luau works out **all** the right-hand values before storing any of them, which makes swapping two variables a one-liner: assign `b, a` to `a, b`.

If there are more names than values, the extra names get `nil`. If there are more values than names, the extras are thrown away. Neither is an error, so count carefully.

sections.heading: Values that never change
sections.body:
Some values are settings rather than state: the delivery fee, the number of deliveries in a shift, the speed of the monster. Scripters usually put these at the top of a script in names written in capitals with underscores, like `DELIVERY_FEE`. Luau doesn't stop you changing them; the capitals are a promise to other readers that you won't.

Keeping settings in one place at the top means you can rebalance your game without hunting through the code. It's one of the simplest habits that makes a project easier to work on.

key_points: `x += 1` means `x = x + 1`. Every arithmetic operator has a compound version.
`..=` appends text to a string variable.
Multiple assignment evaluates every right-hand value first, which makes swaps easy.
Settings that never change go at the top, in capitals.
mistakes: Using `..=` on a variable that's still `nil`.
Scattering magic numbers through a script instead of naming them at the top.
lessons.try_it: Start a variable at 100 coins, then use compound assignment to add a tip, subtract a fee and double the result, printing after each step. Then swap two variables in one line and print both.

quiz.question: What is `x` after `local x = 10` then `x -= 3` then `x *= 2`?
After `local a, b = 1, 2` and then `a, b = b, a`, what are `a` and `b`?
quiz.explain: Luau evaluates both right-hand values before storing, so the values swap.

quiz.question: Why would you write `local MAX_ORDERS = 10` in capitals?
choices: Capitals stop it from being changed
It signals a setting that the code won't change
quiz.explain: It's a naming convention for constants. Luau doesn't enforce it.
